Brain-inspired Neuromorphic Computing uses a bottom-up approach to design
hardware architectures based on biological models and the physical properties
of devices, particularly focusing on memristors. These components mimic the
functions of biological neurons and synapses, enabling the creation of hardware
neural networks capable of performing complex tasks efficiently and autonomously.
In this paper, we introduce SimNAC, a tool for evaluating the performance of
memristive devices and neuromorphic frameworks, allowing users to experiment with
different architectural configurations, device parameters, and learning schemes,
ultimately providing insights into the effects of device variability and network
design on system behavior. Our instrument is a valuable resource for researchers
investigating the potential of memristive devices in neuromorphic applications. SimNAC's capabilities are exemplified through a case study, analyzing the behavior of memristive CMOS systems under various conditions, such as device variability and learning scheme design. Notably, simulations were conducted using a single-core CPU, demonstrating the tool's efficiency. Our results show that large-scale neuromorphic systems can tolerate moderate device variability, but experience significant performance degradation in the presence of systematic variations. Furthermore, experiments using stochastic learning schemes revealed that systems adapt to individual device characteristics, while simulations with mean-teaching algorithms are highly resistant to variability, but vulnerable to systematic device deviations. These findings highlight the importance of thorough system design and careful learning scheme selection to achieve optimal performance in neuromorphic hardware. Notably, SimNAC enabled these in-depth investigations within a reasonable simulation time of around 30 minutes on a single-core CPU. Our tool is now publicly available and can be accessed through the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/STHLab-UPV/SimNAC. Additionally, a detailed user guide can be found in the associated GitHub repository. Lastly, we would like to acknowledge the support provided by the European Research Council under grant 922. Human creativity in describing concepts through metaphors is a unique form of understanding.  Despite their importance in human cognition, visual metaphor analysis by computers remains an unexplored area.  To address this gap, we created a large collection of 5,000 metaphor datasets, known as MetaCLUE, which consists of 2,500 metaphor collections and 2,500 concept-idea pairs.  MetaCLUE is a valuable resource for visual metaphor research due to its extensive size and diversity.  To showcase its potential, we used the dataset to perform three tasks: 1) detecting the dominant concept in each metaphor, 2) identifying key components of the concept, and 3) classifying the style of the metaphor.  The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our dataset and associated methods in visual metaphor research.  Additionally, we plan to make MetaCLUE publicly available to foster further research in this area.  To facilitate this, we will also release the code of our evaluation experiments.  To our knowledge, MetaCLUE is the largest available collection of visual metaphors, offering unparalleled opportunities for visual metaphor analysis.  As such, it will be an invaluable resource for researchers in the field of computer-based metaphor analysis.  MetaCLUE can be accessed at https://research.google.com/pubs/pub?s=Qs5yMQ.  The code used for the analysis is available at https://github.com/zheduozo/MetaCLUE.  To learn more about the dataset, visit https://research.google.com/brain/team_meeting/MetaCLUE.htm.

A significant body of research has shown that higher language model accuracy often results in more accurate predictions of human reading behavior. However, recent studies have revealed that this relationship does not consistently hold true for various language processing tasks, including the forecasting of reading times. This study examines the correlation between human reading times and the predictions generated by larger transformer-based language models, such as BERT, RoBERTa, and XLNet, across multiple datasets. The findings indicate that while earlier models show a good match with human performance, this alignment is compromised by larger models. This discrepancy can be attributed to two factors: (1) the limitations in capturing higher-order information in text by focusing solely on input tokens, and (2) the computational inefficiencies of attention mechanisms used in transformer-based models, which hinder their ability to process extensive contextual information. The study also suggests that future research should focus on developing a comprehensive understanding of human reading behavior and incorporating this knowledge into predictive models. This approach may lead to the creation of more accurate language processing systems that closely mirror human cognition. As a consequence, the vast majority of internet attacks are now botnet-related, highlighting the need for effective tools to detect these threats. One such approach involves analyzing patterns of activity on servers to identify botnet groups and their command sequences, which we achieve by leveraging machine learning techniques for text analysis. Our proposed method involves converting honeypot command logs into standardized formats, followed by the application of text classification techniques to distinguish botnet activity from genuine user commands. Through the use of a machine learning pipeline and comparison with conventional methods, we demonstrate the potential of our approach to accurately classify commands and distinguish botnet activity from other internet traffic. Ultimately, we envision the use of this technology to enable real-time analysis of large command log datasets, thereby facilitating the early detection of malicious activity across various internet applications. Our initial results suggest that our approach can accurately distinguish between botnet and human commands, and even identify distinct command patterns emanating from different IP sources. By applying this technique to a broad range of internet applications, we believe that we can further enhance its effectiveness in detecting and mitigating malicious activity. This research introduces two novel graph-based metrics - the fundamental matrix and dual fundamental matrix - each defined as average distances between any two nodes. These measures effectively capture various network characteristics. Derived from the Erdös-Rényi random graph, these matrices offer characteristics similar to the Laplacian matrix, with properties that support orthogonal decomposition and a form of eigenvector transformation. Additionally, they enable the development of a network's combinatorial dual representation, facilitating the analysis and computation of this dual representation. An algorithm is provided to calculate the fundamental and dual fundamental distances in real-world graphs. Furthermore, this study applies these metrics to quantify small-world phenomena in real-world networks. All associated data is publicly available for further investigation. Lastly, future applications and potential research paths are also explored. Two related R packages, netmetrics and duMST, facilitate the computation of these metrics, allowing for in-depth network analysis. Brain neoplasm segmentation from MRI data is a complex task due to the diseases' varied presentations and similarities in appearance between tumors and normal brain tissue. To improve segmentation performance, we introduce a novel 3D U-Net architecture, which incorporates contextual information through a 2D convolutional layer applied to the input MRI volume. This layer provides a feature map highlighting difficulty areas, guiding a subsequent attention module to concentrate on the input data within the network. Our experiments on the BraTS 2018 dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving new benchmarks in dice, hauka and performance metrics. This 3D UNET-based network proves to be a versatile and efficient solution for brain tumor segmentation. Moreover, our proposed method's source code is publicly available on the GitHub platform. https://github.com/jeanpanjean/Context3DUNET. This implementation includes two main functions: the 3D U-Net for brain tumor segmentation and a visualization tool to display the network's output. Additionally, we provide an example of a containerized application using Docker, facilitating deployment on local machines. A detailed step-by-step guide is available in a separate document. https://github.com/jeanpanjean/Context3DUNET/blob/master/docs/running_the_container.pdf. In conclusion, our experiments confirm the robustness and efficiency of our proposed method, outperforming the baseline model and achieving superior results. This study introduces a randomized, orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) technique, referred to as Rand-OFDM, for enhanced security in wireless data transmission. By randomly modifying the frequency spectrum of each data symbol, rather than only the phase, Rand-OFDM increases secrecy for both single and multiple users. Compared to standard OFDM, Rand-OFDM offers greater security against phase-based attacks. Furthermore, the performance degradation associated with Rand-OFDM is minimal, making it an attractive solution for secure data transmission across various wireless networks. An example simulation is provided to illustrate the application of Rand-OFDM in a cellular system. Additionally, the study explores the potential of combining Rand-OFDM with existing security measures to create a more comprehensive security framework for wireless data transmission. An experimental evaluation of Rand-OFDM is conducted using software-defined radio platforms. The results demonstrate the feasibility of implementing Rand-OFDM in practical wireless data transmission systems. The findings suggest that Rand-OFDM could be a valuable addition to existing security protocols, such as physical layer security (PLS) and physical layer security over fading channels (F-PLS), for enhancing the security of data transmission in wireless networks. An extensive comparison of Rand-OFDM with existing security measures is conducted, including a detailed analysis of its performance in comparison to traditional OFDM. The study concludes with recommendations for potential future research directions. An accompanying video demonstrates the technique's application in a cellular system. Network-based tree-structure models are frequently employed to analyze clustered data, and their applicability extends to fields like computer vision, linguistics, and social networks.  We propose a set of methods for analyzing tree-structure models, enabling the assessment of a tree's structural elements and their impact on model fit.  Our approach also provides a way to determine the number of nodes in a tree, and to compare tree structures across multiple models.  Notably, our methods can be used not only as standalone tools but also as a basis for developing various statistical techniques, including model selection and estimation.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods through simulation studies and a real-world analysis of a large document corpus.  Our R package, modEx, provides implemented solutions for our proposed methods.  Furthermore, our work contributes to the theoretical fields of network modeling and model selection, offering new insights and approaches for these domains.  Our R package's documentation can be found at https://www.ricardoquintos.com/modEx.  A preprint version of this article is available at arXiv. This thesis focuses on developing a system for identifying objects within complex images like forms, bank statements, and slides, which are characterized by their diverse backgrounds and multiple irrelevant elements. A novel approach called the Integrated Dataset and Classifier (IDC) framework is introduced, combining weakly-supervised learning with a clustering technique to automatically categorize and learn object classes from large datasets. IDc leverages the unique characteristics of bag-of-visual-words models by applying spatial pooling to generate a sparse matrix representing feature vectors. Furthermore, this approach enables the automatic creation of multiple object classes for improved object recognition accuracy. Performance evaluations using several large datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in visual object recognition for forms and slides. Additionally, IDc is capable of learning object classes without manual supervision, making it a valuable tool for applications like content-based image retrieval in document images. Furthermore, IDc can be adapted to other complex image recognition tasks like text detection and identification. Finally, this thesis proposes a new dataset for evaluating object recognition in slide images. It features 10,000 manually annotated images with 1,500 identified objects across 10 different object classes. These images are derived from a dataset of 40,000 images collected from a total of 400 slides. The dataset and associated code can be found at https://github.com/umonsees/IDC. while maintaining the model's accuracy, by identifying and eliminating the least important calculations.

which show that it significantly reduces computational costs without compromising performance compared to smaller models.

while incurring only a minimal fraction of the original training costs. The source code for GF-T is publicly available.

Research in imitation learning has shifted focus from generative adversarial networks to using behavioral cloning with expert feedback, particularly through off-policy experience collection using Importance Weighted Actor-Critic methods.  A new approach, SoftDICE, enhances IWAC methods by incorporating a penalty to steer collections towards the expert's distribution, rather than just matching it, which in turn boosts imitation learning performance by collecting a more comprehensive range of experiences during the training process.  This approach, demonstrated on benchmarks such as Procgen and DeepMind Control, results in notable improvements of 2.5-4.5% in average task reward, with notable enhancements in tasks featuring complex dynamics like Procgen BasketBall and DeepMind CartPole SwingUp.  A detailed analysis of SoftDICE reveals that it can be viewed as a variant of IWAC methods with enhanced generalizability, and that it naturally balances sample efficiency and data efficiency by promoting a more diverse set of experiences during the training process.  A simple variant of SoftDICE, specifically the SoftDICE-SR method, has been found to match or surpass the performance of IWAC and other leading methods, such as VIME, without requiring sophisticated hyperparameter tuning.  This method, SoftDICE-SR, can be easily implemented with minimal hyperparameter adjustments, and it is set to become a preferred choice for imitation learning.  A corresponding code implementation of SoftDICE and SoftDICE-SR is now available online for use and further exploration.  The code can be accessed at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/rlkit/rlkit/blob/master/rlkit/utils SoftDICE.py. This research explores a newly proposed concept of coprimeness in linear discrete systems, distinct from existing approaches. The novel definition of coprimeness is developed through the S-polynomial method, revealing its equivalence to a subset of the rank condition in system decoupling. Additionally, a necessary condition for coprimeness is identified, along with a proposed criterion based on irreducible graphs of the system's implicit equations. However, it is noted that this criterion remains inconclusive. A fundamental question arising from this concept is posed, inquiring whether the absence of common factors among the components of a discrete system guarantees the existence of a corresponding basis. In response, a proposed answer is grounded in a previously established theorem by Janet's algorithm. A distinguishing feature of this concept of coprimeness is also highlighted. Furthermore, a proposed algorithm for determining coprimeness is presented. The application of this concept is demonstrated in the context of algebraic cryptology, where a proposed encryption scheme utilizing discrete systems meets the criteria of confidentiality, verifiability, and key security. The encryption scheme is demonstrated through a proposed algorithm, utilizing coprimeness as a critical component. The security of this scheme is further reinforced by an analysis of its potential vulnerability to certain attacks. The potential for generalization of this concept is also explored, drawing inspiration from existing research in this area. The research concludes by highlighting opportunities for future investigation and applications of this newly proposed concept of coprimeness. Deep neural networks often produce features that are highly redundant. To address this issue, we propose a new approach called IRC (In-Training Representation Correlation). During the training process, IRC identifies and eliminates redundant information by comparing image representations generated by the convolutional layers. Since these representations are created during training, we use a surrogate loss to minimize the correlation between them, making our features less redundant. Despite achieving impressive results in various tasks, the underlying principles of deep learning's remarkable performance are not yet fully understood. This paper aims to clarify some aspects of this phenomenon, specifically by drawing on concepts from interpolation theory and regression. It proposes that the key to successful machine learning lies in a small, carefully constructed dataset that inherently contains the solution to a given problem. This insight is supported by several observations, including the fact that deep learning models excel at tasks where the training data closely resembles the distribution of the test data; the ability of these models to learn even with minimal training data; and their tendency to 'overfit' in expected ways. These phenomena can be explained by the 'interpolation interpolation hypothesis', which posits that small datasets typically contain multiple possible solutions, while larger datasets tend to have only one viable solution. Furthermore, the paper investigates the mathematical properties of interpolation tasks and notes that deep learning models often converge to the same solution as linear methods, although they may employ non-linear techniques. This insight is reinforced by the observation of 'interpolation paths', where small changes in a dataset's size result in proportional changes in the model's weights. These observations are not unique to deep learning and can be observed in other models that rely on interpolation. Finally, the paper discusses the potential implications of this line of thinking for future research into mathematical approaches to learning. To translate between languages with limited data, a new approach called cross-modal alignment is proposed, which enables efficient use of related languages' signals. This method combines neural machine translation systems in a single network, allowing the simultaneous translation between not only the original language pairs but also other language pairs that share similar characteristics. Experimental results demonstrate that this multi-task training method significantly enhances translation performance in low-resource settings. Furthermore, a developed visual interface facilitates the selection of related languages and fine-tuning of our system with minimal user interaction, requiring no expertise in language technology. This interface enables the effective exploitation of available linguistic data to improve translation performance without requiring additional resources. Experimental evaluations on various language pairs from the language family, specifically those in Slavic and Indo-Aryan, as well as non-cognates, show substantial improvements in translation quality. On the WMT 2015 English-Croatian translation task, our model outperformed the most recent state-of-the-art results by 3.5 BLEU scores, while on the WMT 2017 English-Czech translation task, we achieved a 1.7 BLEU score improvement. Moreover, our method allows for the easy addition of new related language pairs to our system, enhancing translation performance in domains with limited data, such as the language combination of English and Romanian, where we achieved a 2.5 BLEU score improvement. This method's effectiveness is also demonstrated in scenarios where a single model is trained for multiple language pairs, eliminating the need for manual data selection and enabling efficient language pair transfer. A novel method for multi-view object detection is presented, which utilizes a voxelized feature aggregation approach to enhance performance. By first dividing a stereo image pair into 3D voxels, the method calculates a characteristic value based on the contents of each voxel. These characteristic values are then aggregated across voxels to facilitate object detection. The novel method achieves this by dividing the 3D voxel grid into 8x8x8 sub-volumes and computing 3x3x3 characteristic values based on the mean, standard deviation, and count of stereo image pixels. These values are then aggregated across the 8x8x8 sub-volumes to generate a 3D voxelized feature, which serves as input for object detection. The proposed voxelized characteristic aggregation approach is evaluated on the KITTI 3D scene parsing and nuScenes vehicle tracking benchmarks, demonstrating its state-of-the-art performance. Additionally, the method's adaptability is demonstrated through its successful application to the BDD100K autonomous driving benchmark. The proposed voxelized characteristic aggregation approach is made available as an open-source PyTorch implementation. Further details are available at https://github.com/DAER-GPRL/char-aggregation. and https://www.nuscenes.org/. Accurate measurement of the left venticle's dimensions is crucial for assessing cardiac function, but manual analysis is prone to errors resulting from variations in heart shape and imaging quality. This paper introduces a new method for measuring left venticle dimensions that is more robust and automatic, relying on a three-dimensional steerable pyramid transformation to analyze the left venticle cavity from a long-axis echocardiographic view. By decomposing the signal into 10 orientation-selective sub-bands, the proposed method facilitates dimension extraction and calculation of the left venticle's shape parameters. Experiments using 100 echocardiographic videos with manually annotated dimensions demonstrated that this approach outperforms traditional methods, with improved dimension measurement accuracy and reduced sensitivity to heart shape and imaging quality variations. Furthermore, the proposed method yields similar left venticle volume estimates as manual analysis but reduces the time required for calculation. It also outperforms existing edge detection-based methods in volume estimates while being more efficient. Overall, the proposed method improves heart function assessment by making it easier to extract accurate left venticle dimensions from echocardiographic images. causing variations in limit loads due to changes in limit loads' magnitudes and types.
This work introduces Resilient Limit Assessment Theory (RLAT), a method to evaluate 
a structure's limit load under uncertainty, enabling the evaluation of the worst-case 
limit load for a given distribution of material property uncertainties. This is achieved 
through the use of limit loads' resilience curves, which are essential for RLAT's 
underpinnings and its implementation as detailed in this paper. This theory also 
facilitates the development of a method for computing worst-case limit loads and 
providing insights into the resilience curves' characteristics. This method is versatile 
and can be applied to various structural finite element analysis problems with 
consideration for material property uncertainties. Additionally, RLAT is also capable of 
providing worst-case limit loads for spatial and statistical uncertainties in loads. 
RLAT is demonstrated through numerical examples to verify its accuracy. This theory is 
expected to serve as a valuable tool for engineers to assess the resilience of structures 
under uncertainty. This is in contrast to traditional limit analysis methods, which 
focus on evaluating limit loads under deterministic conditions. This theory is also 
expected to be useful in the evaluation of structures with uncertainties, which is a

Vision-based classification networks have become particularly effective, especially in the field of bird species identification. This process involved two initial tasks: binarizing bird species into either perching or non-perching birds, and categorizing bird species into distinct groups. Importantly, this research demonstrates that multistage classification outperforms single-stage classification in the final task, with notable improvements in accuracy. This work also highlights the challenges of balancing classes within multistage classification and presents strategies for addressing these issues. Furthermore, this study emphasizes the importance of multistage classification in bird species categorization, especially in the context of conservation efforts. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the development of efficient methods for multistage classification, with potential applications extending beyond bird species categorization. to nonsymmetric systems, allowing for the efficient solution of regularized saddle-position
systems. This method is further enhanced by a derived error bound, which estimates
the sub-optimality in the minimax lower bound associated with the system's optimal
solution. The efficacy of KRCSP methods is demonstrated through numerical results,

conventional preconditioned Krylov methods, IP-NASTRAN solvers, and RAS methods.,

groundwater flow models, thereby underscoring their potential value in practical
applications. The KRCSP solvers have been implemented in a public repository. The

This study explores the asymptotic properties of a stochastic linear equation in the form of dXt = L*tXt + dNt, where L is a positive definite operator in an M-dimensional space, and N is a Gaussian white noise. We identify two primary scenarios: a standard model where L can be represented as the product of n distinct eigenvalues, and a more general case in which L can be represented as the sum of eigenvalues within a specific range of positive and negative values. We establish that these two models yield the same large deviation principle, and derive the associated limit theorems for the equation's solution. Specifically, we show that its distribution converges to a multivariate Gaussian distribution under certain conditions. We also introduce a new concept of "roughness" for the Gaussian noise N, and demonstrate that its corresponding stochastic equation exhibits distinct asymptotic behavior. Interestingly, the equation's behavior is more complex in the rough case, and its associated limit theorems are formulated differently compared to the standard case. Ultimately, the results presented in this study provide a comprehensive understanding of the equation's asymptotic behavior and highlight the distinct characteristics of the rough model. Additionally, the study's findings have practical implications for the corresponding stochastic partial differential equations in the context of the Navier-Stokes equations. A companion paper by Mohan will explore the application of the derived results to the Navier-Stokes equations. A significant challenge in machine learning is handling datasets that contain a substantial number of very sparse positive instances, making it difficult to establish a positive class. Positive-Unlabeled Learning (PUL) is a method that redefines the classification task as distinguishing between positive and unlabeled data. However, traditional PUL models struggle with making the most of available unlabeled information, resulting in subpar performance. To address this limitation, we propose a novel self-supervised approach for PUL, dubbed PUL-Sup. This method leverages self-supervised positive representation learning to enhance the effectiveness of PUL models. Our approach is validated through extensive experiments on real-world datasets, demonstrating its superiority over previous PUL models. Furthermore, ablation studies and visualizations confirm that self-supervised learning plays a pivotal role in improving performance. Our code and datasets are made publicly available at https://github.com/THUML/THM-PUL-Sup. Additionally, we have identified a limitation of our method in handling datasets with both highly imbalanced and varying class densities. To mitigate this, we propose a PUL model with a hybrid loss function that incorporates a balanced negative sampling strategy. The results of our experiments on multiple imbalanced datasets confirm the effectiveness of our approach. The corresponding code is available at https://github.com/THML/THM-PUL-HL. Videos illustrating the method and results are also provided at https://youtu.be/7q5s5iZjKQs and https://youtu.be/5k5s5iZjKQs. Moreover, we have identified a generalization issue in PUL models due to a lack of robustness in training. To mitigate this, we propose a PUL model with a PUL-assisted data augmentation (PULDA) approach. The method is also evaluated on multiple public datasets, demonstrating its superiority over previous PUL models. Our code is available at https://github.com/THML/THM-PUL-DA. Videos illustrating the method and results are also provided at https://youtu.be/7q5s5iZjKQs and https://youtu.be/5k5s5iZjKQs. Finally, we have developed a PUL model with a PUL-assisted knowledge distillation (PULKD) approach. The method is also evaluated on multiple public datasets, demonstrating its superiority over previous PUL models. Our code is available at https://github.com/THML/THM-PUL-KD.

Hartman and Overmeyer's 1979 conjecture asserts that creating a simple polygon by connecting disjoint line segments, subject to the constraint that the resulting polygon has a bounded number of vertices, is an NP-hard problem. We present a proof of this conjecture. Furthermore, we establish that determining the minimum number of line segments required to form a simple polygon with $n$ vertices is also NP-hard. This problem is equivalent to the minimum feedback vertex covering problem in graphs, making our proof straightforward. We also demonstrate the NP-hardness of a related problem related to the edge covering of graphs. Finally, we explore some additional applications of our main result. To address this issue, researchers have developed various domain adaptation techniques that help re-ID models learn from a single domain source and generalize to multiple target domains. However, the current domain adaptation methods for re-ID are limited in their ability to handle complex camera clusters and domain-specific variations in feature representations. To address this issue, this research proposes a novel unsupervised domain adaptation method for re-ID, incorporating a two-stage training approach that involves clustering the domain-specific features and aligning these clusters at the attribute level. To achieve this, the proposed method employs a two-stage training process, first learning a feature extractor that can identify person identities across different domains, and then aligning the domain-specific clusters based on attribute-level information. Experimental results on three large-scale re-ID datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, achieving state-of-the-art performance on these datasets. Notably, the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, reducing the rank-1 accuracy gap by 3.2%, 3.6%, and 4.2% on Market-1501, DukeMTMC-MVe, and DukeMTMC-ReID datasets respectively. In this research, we investigate a type of Voronoi map that incorporates stable matching constraints among its vertices and edges. This practical example reveals that in stable-matching Voronai maps, the stable matching constraints can significantly impede the efficiency of traditional algorithms for shortest path calculations. Furthermore, we investigate the resilience of classification models when faced with adversarial data and find that certain models are more robust than others. Importantly, our research suggests that even simple training data can be used to effectively defend against these types of attacks, which holds promise for real-world applications. We believe that our findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of the adversarial robustness of classification models. Finally, we discuss the implications of our research for practical fraud detection scenarios. The main objective of this research is to establish a numerical solution to an inverse coefficient problem for the Riemannian Radiative Transfer Equation. The challenge arises from irregular boundary data and an unknown internal region, with an underlying assumption that the transfer coefficient varies consistently throughout the interior and relies on a specific Riemannian metric. To address this complex problem, we develop a novel, two-stage approach. Firstly, we transform the underlying problem into a more manageable form, then implement a convexification technique to ensure the solution's uniqueness. Secondly, we construct a functional space that allows us to accurately approximate the solution, and ultimately use a combination of Fourier analysis and a nonlinear optimization method to obtain the solution. Our approach is supported by numerical examples that demonstrate its effectiveness in reconstructing coefficients and visual representations of the internal region from external data. Interestingly, we find that the transfer coefficient's internal structure mirrors the characteristics of the underlying Riemannian metric, providing valuable insights for modeling the underlying metric. This research lays the groundwork for further investigation into numerical solutions to inverse coefficient problems for complex equations, such as the reaction-diffusion equation. Furthermore, we explore the potential for adapting our approach to tackle similar problems involving the Helmholtz and Laplace equation. Ultimately, we hope to apply our developed methodology to real-world applications in medical and geophysical imaging. Additionally, we plan to expand the scope of our approach to tackle more complex inverse coefficient problems involving multiple unknowns and boundary data, and to obtain accurate approximations of the solution. The outcomes of this research will contribute to a deeper understanding of the relationship between coefficients and data in mathematical models, and ultimately lead to new practical applications in various fields. The corresponding numerical code will be made publicly available. The research will culminate in a PhD thesis. This research presents an innovative approach to pan-sharpening using deep gradient estimation networks (DGES), which leverage the residual error between low-resolution and high-resolution images to generate a high-resolution image. By employing this method, the need for explicit model optimization is eliminated, and the method can adapt to any distribution of residual error between images. The DGES method consists of two distinct components: a residual error estimation network that predicts residual maps from input images and a fusion network that generates a high-resolution image from these predicted maps. Notably, the method can accommodate any image type, including pansar, multispectral, and hyper-spectral data. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through experiments conducted on three distinct datasets, resulting in superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have achieved notable success in processing graph-structured data, but they have significant limitations due to their inherent lack of discriminative power, which can lead to a failure to distinguish between similar and dissimilar graph pairs. To address this issue, we introduce a novel discriminative propagation (DP) rule that can be seamlessly integrated into any GNN framework. This DP rule is based on a unique approach to propagating node features, which involves a node's neighbors receiving features that reflect both the node's inherent characteristics and the similarities between the node and its neighbors. By leveraging this DP rule, our proposed NODE-SELECT framework can effectively identify the most critical nodes in a graph. Experimental results on diverse datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method, which can be easily extended to handle multi-class node classification tasks. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed DP rule and NODE-SELECT framework, particularly in scenarios where nodes have similar features. Deep learning neural networks have achieved impressive success in numerous image recognition tasks, such as identifying objects, facial expressions, and medical images. However, the development of effective image recognition neural networks is often time-consuming, requiring extensive data collection and annotation. When applied to a new domain, such networks may not perform well due to differences in imaging conditions, noise levels, and sensor degradation. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed various deep learning techniques for adapting neural networks to new domains. This study compares the effectiveness of several transfer domain methods, including domain random initialization, domain adaptation through self-supervised learning, and fine-tuning pre-trained models, on various image recognition tasks. Our results demonstrate that domain random initialization and self-supervised learning are not sufficient to improve performance in most cases. In contrast, fine-tuning pre-trained models yields better results, but only when the pre-trained and target domains share similar data distribution characteristics. These findings have important implications for the development of deep learning models in real-world medical imaging applications. These new findings not only provide a unified solution to the SL(3,Z) modular form problem but also offer a valuable tool for further research, allowing for the extension of our expression to the broader class of indefinite, simply connected lattices and the calculation of the Langlands' local factors for general lattices. Moreover, our work paves the way for the investigation of the SL(3,Z) trace formulas and the computation of the Fourier coefficients of the Eisenstein series, which in turn enables the derivation of the Hecke eigenvalues for the non-cuspidal Eisenstein automorphic forms. Although our approach is not optimized for the practical application, it provides essential insights into the analytical properties of the $L$-functions, specifically their behavior at the critical point $s=\tfrac{1}{2}$. This method can be further refined and optimized to yield a computational formula for the SL(3,Z) $L$-functions, specifically when $s$ is within the critical strip. To facilitate future research, we have compiled a comprehensive list of the calculated terms of the SL(3,Z) $L$-functions, which will be instrumental in the development of the analytical Langlands program. In the context of differential privacy, we address a key challenge by developing a method to efficiently train a model without compromising privacy using stochastic gradient descent and other optimization techniques. We address two primary issues: 1) developing an effective surrogate loss that maintains data privacy and enables efficient training, and 2) establishing a convergence guarantee for noisy optimization in private learning. Our proposed surrogate loss utilizes a combination of empirical risk and a data-dependent term that adapts to the privacy parameter based on the Lipschitz sensitivity of the target loss. Through theoretical analysis, we establish that this modified loss converges to the optimal solution at a rate of $O(\epsilon^{-2})$, and more surprisingly, we also establish a sublinear convergence rate of $O(\epsilon^{-4})$ for this loss. Moreover, we establish a convergence rate of $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ for SGD optimization in the context of this loss. Our results are further validated through empirical testing on various datasets. Our research opens up new possibilities for the application of stochastic gradient descent to private learning in differential privacy, paving the way for future research in this area. A new algorithm called ISLET has been proposed to address the high computational cost of existing methods, which often involve iterative singular value decomposition and gradient descent. processing requirements. To overcome this, we introduce a novel network called

features in 3D point clouds. By focusing on sparse key points, AttDLNet

through ablation studies, we validate the effectiveness of AttDLNet's
architecture and depth-wise attention mechanism. Our code and pre-trained
models are publicly available for further research. Through extensive
experiments, we demonstrate AttDLNet's ability to accurately recognize object
locations in real-world scenarios, including complex urban environments. The
network's performance is impressive, with a 95.5% AP and 10.5 FPS on the

The object-oriented network (OON) is an effective representation for encoding knowledge in the form of interconnected entities linked by functional relationships. Furthermore, we can also leverage the OON to provide recommendations for ingredient substitutions, recipe modifications, and adjustment of nutritional goals. Empirical evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in enhancing recipe safety and enhancing user flexibility when it comes to recipe creation. Temporal link prediction, or forecasting the future graph structure, is a crucial yet underdeveloped area in link forecasting. This task involves predicting the edges that will appear in a graph at a future time. Existing methods typically focus on short-term predictions and rely on connections between nodes, such as physical proximity. This framework is capable of forecasting complex, multi-hop connections and can be applied to various domains, resulting in more accurate predictions. Our proposed method, DisCoBank, utilizes a dynamic knowledge graph to represent node relationships and incorporates an encoder-decoder structure to predict the future graph. This approach is both computationally efficient and scalable. Through extensive testing on real-world datasets, DisCoDB significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 10-20% improvement in accuracy. This research has significant potential to enhance a wide range of applications, including social network analysis, knowledge graph completion, and recommender systems. This paper introduces a first-order constraint solver that can handle multibody systems, utilizing a novel approach to finite difference approximation. By leveraging absolute stability, this method can effectively manage non-linear constraints, such as those from rigid body kinematics and elasticity. We demonstrate the solvers' efficacy through simulations involving both smaller and larger test systems, in addition to applying it to a complex car chassis system. Results show that the solver maintains stability even at large time steps, offering a desirable property for real-time applications. Furthermore, its miscalibration-resistant nature allows for accurate simulations without prior knowledge of the integrator's error. By contrast to second-order methods, whose step sizes are constrained by their order, our solver's larger time steps and lower computational costs make it an attractive alternative. We validate these benefits through performance comparisons and analyses of simulation accuracy. Lastly, we highlight potential avenues for enhancing simulation robustness and efficiency. This study investigates the effectiveness and stability of optimization methods that combine differential privacy with traditional regularization techniques, focusing on linear regression and support vector machines. By analyzing the outcomes of these methods, we can identify scenarios where DP provides valuable insights and can be effectively integrated. Conversely, we also discuss situations where DP may not be necessary or could even hinder results. Through a comprehensive analysis, we aim to determine the optimal DP parameters that balance data utility and privacy protection. Specifically, we explore the influence of DP on support vector machines and show that it significantly impacts the model's decision boundary, which in turn affects the margin and classification accuracy. Using this understanding, we develop a simple strategy for selecting the optimal DP parameters based on the underlying noise distribution and domain characteristics. Finally, we demonstrate the practical application of these findings by applying them to real-world problems, including hyperparameter tuning for optimization with DP. Through numerical simulations, we observe that the proposed method yields better privacy-utility trade-offs compared to existing DP optimization techniques. Ultimately, we conclude that DP is particularly valuable in situations where model overfitting is a concern, and it can be effectively integrated with regularization techniques to achieve this effect. However, we also emphasize that DP is not essential in scenarios where sufficient regularization is already present. As a result, we recommend exercising caution when applying DP to optimization problems and selecting the optimal DP parameters based on the specific characteristics of the model. Conversational search systems require a crucial component: a dynamic keyword extraction (KWE) mechanism that can adapt to user input in real-time. This paper revisits the traditional document retrieval framework and integrates a real-time KWE element to improve its effectiveness. We examine the current approaches to KWE and propose a novel, two-stage method that leverages the user's query to extract relevant keywords. The method comprises a keyword candidate generation stage and a keyword selection stage. In the first stage, we employ a neural model to identify potential keywords from the user's query, and in the second stage, we utilize a neural model to determine the most relevant keywords from the search results. Experimental results on a conversational web search dataset demonstrate the superiority of our two-stage approach over existing methods. The performance gap between our method and the state-of-the-art baselines is substantial, and we observe that our proposed KWE element enhances the overall conversational search performance. The code and dataset used in this study are publicly available. The findings of this work can be applied to enhance conversational search systems and serve as a starting point for future research in the integration of real-time KWE with traditional retrieval models. Researchers have proposed various methods for learning predicate discovery, but most of these approaches focus on extracting high-level features from low-level image or text data. Conversely, we will demonstrate the efficacy of using prediction errors to inform and enhance machine learning models. By leveraging these errors, we can implement a feedback mechanism that significantly improves the performance of predicate discovery models. Specifically, we will apply this error-driven approach to a state-of-the-art method for learning predicates from image data, and will also introduce a novel technique for learning predicates from text data. Our results indicate that incorporating this error-based feedback mechanism leads to substantial performance enhancements. Furthermore, we will apply our approach to a real-world task, namely, identifying the locations of dress items in shopping cart images. This application showcases that even when models are trained on visual data, the errors can be used to inform text-based predicate discovery, ultimately enhancing overall system performance. Our work is particularly relevant to tasks where models operate in different data domains. For instance, in image captioning, the model's errors can be used to improve text-based predicate discovery, leading to better image understanding. Similarly, in image-based tasks, the errors can be used to improve image-based predicate discovery, leading to better text interpretation. In the field of high-energy physics, researchers utilize data analysis to investigate various aspects of particle interactions. Researchers in LHCb collaborate to analyze large datasets obtained from its 12-year run, producing numerous subdatasets that are later merged for comprehensive analysis. These subdatasets are stored in separate HDF5 files, which are commonly used to organize scientific data due to their efficiency and reliability. However, merging these files can be time-consuming and resource-intensive, especially when dealing with substantial datasets. This research aims to optimize the merging process by implementing parallelism through multi-threaded execution. We present a case study merging 100 large HDF5 files at CERN, utilizing up to 16 CPU cores, which demonstrates significant speedup in merging performance when compared to sequential execution. The associated source code is publicly accessible on GitHub.

The tautaubar system, primarily responsible for the background, exhibits a distinct two-body decay pattern, whereas the primary higgsino signal is characterized by a softer decay pattern due to the presence of a third-missing particle component. By analyzing the angular distributions of the decay products, it is possible to distinguish between the signal and background, with the former displaying a pronounced peaking behavior. Our study demonstrates that, through a careful selection of the jet radius and the transverse momentum of the charged leptons, the resulting tautaubar background can be effectively separated from the higgsino signal. Furthermore, we investigate the potential benefits of utilizing jet grooming techniques, such as soft drop, to enhance the signal-to-background ratio. Our findings indicate that, in the presence of a $100\,{\rm GeV}$ higgsino, an optimal set of jet radii and jet grooming parameters could increase the signal-to-background ratio by a factor of up to $2.5$. Conversely, for a $500\,{\rm GeV}$ higgsino, a similar improvement in the signal-to-background ratio may be achieved with a smaller jet radius, but a lower jet grooming parameter. Our analysis also reveals that, for both higgsino masses, an optimal set of jet radii and jet grooming parameters could yield a signal-to-background ratio greater than $10$ at the LHC with a $300\,{\rm GeV}$ center-of-mass energy. However, for a $300\,{\rm GeV}$ center-of-mass energy, the signal-to-background ratio would be less than $10$ regardless of the chosen jet radius and jet grooming parameters. In the context of graph optimization, we explore the challenge of minimizing the assemblage of shortest paths connecting source-destination pairs of a graph. Specifically, this involves adding edges to a graph to reduce the overall complexity of its paths. We demonstrate that this problem falls under the FRP framework, which seeks to optimize the fractional dimension of shortest paths. Building on previous research, we establish that incorporating random edge additions can optimize the minimal assemblage for a graph. We also introduce a novel algorithm that utilizes reinforcement learning to predict the effectiveness of edge additions and drive the minimal assemblage process forward. Through extensive testing, we confirm that this approach successfully promotes low-dimensional shortest paths and outperforms established methods in both artificial and real-world graph simulations. The research also sheds light on the relationship between path dimensionality and the minimal assemblage process, revealing that a lower fractional dimension correlates with a more efficient minimal assemblage. Furthermore, our findings indicate that a graph's path dimension is influenced by its connectivity, with highly connected graphs exhibiting lower path dimensions. We also observe that a graph's path dimension remains stable as the minimal assemblage process unfolds, suggesting that a fixed graph structure can be reached. The research concludes with a discussion of potential applications of this work in graph optimization and network design. Ultimately, this research paves the way for future investigations of graph optimization problems, including the development of novel algorithms and the analysis of graph connectivity. In the realm of speedrunning, players aim to execute intricate sequences of actions at an exceptionally high pace within a given game, often pushing the limits of what is considered feasible. Traditionally, this feat is achieved by players themselves, but researchers are now working on developing artificial intelligence (AI) systems that can automate these actions and deliver near-optimal performance. This paper serves as an overview of the speedrunning community's distinctive characteristics, with a specific focus on how these dynamics impact speedrun AI. For a deeper understanding, we examine notable examples of AI research applied to popular games, and discuss the unique challenges presented by each. Finally, this paper identifies key areas of focus for future work in the field of speedrun AI.

We investigate the computational complexity of the Cycles problem, which involves listing all cycles in a graph, and the Hamiltonian Cycle problem, which entails constructing a cycle that visits each vertex exactly once. Notably, these problems are known to be NP-hard, precluding the possibility of an efficient algorithm running in polynomial time for all cases. However, for graphs embedded in 2D space, we establish that Cycles and Hamiltonian Cycle can be solved in less than exponential time when considering a graph with more than 1,672,839 vertices. Furthermore, our approach can be adapted to handle graphs in three-dimensional space or realizations of three-dimensional graphs in two dimensions, assuming the graphs have a planar layout. To achieve this, our algorithm utilizes a combination of techniques, including dynamic programming, approximate cycle representations, and algorithms for counting and enumerating cycles. We introduce Nadir and Broad-swath Altimeter Data Interpolation (N/BADI), 
an end-to-end model that uses a 4DVar network to directly predict altimetric data. 
This model addresses the traditional issue of separating nadir and broad-swath data into independent fields, 
and instead leverages their interconnectedness. 
By training on a dataset of synthetic altimetric measurements, we achieve optimal performance, 
with evaluation metrics indicating a 0.2 cm root mean square error. Compared to conventional methods, 
N/BADI demonstrates a 4.5% reduction in root mean square error. 
This model also exhibits strong generalization capabilities, 
with synthetic data interpolation results showing high accuracy and consistency, even when using unseen swaths. 
Furthermore, N/BADI can be easily adapted to real-world altimetric datasets, 
with applications including satellite data assimilation and ocean modeling. 
This work marks a significant advancement towards more accurate and efficient altimetry data assimilation. 
Future research will explore the application of N/BADI to real-world altimetric data.

We examine the $c$-variant spectrum of power functions over finite fields $\mathbb{F}_q$, focusing on the behavior of polynomials of the form $f(x) = x^k + c$, with $c$ a non-zero element of the field $\Gamma_q$ (excluding $0$). We derive general characterizations of $c$-variant spectra for any given $k$ using polynomials, known as generalized polynomials, within $\Gamma_q$. Additionally, we provide explicit and efficient methods for constructing all possible $c$-variant spectra of power functions. Furthermore, we provide examples of power functions on $\mathbb{F}_q^{n}$ that possess a substantial number of distinct $c$-variant spectra. We also investigate the relationship between $c$-variant spectra and the number of rational points on a specific type of variety known as the $c$-covering variety. Our work provides a complete solution to an existing problem proposed by Kuleshov and Sotirova. We also establish a connection between the number of $c$-variant spectra and the number of rational points on the mentioned variety, showing that these two quantities are equivalent. We also prove that the total number of generalized polynomials is equal to the number of $c$-variant spectra of power functions. We derive explicit upper and lower bounds for these quantities, and show that the established bounds are tight. Finally, we provide a new construction of generalized polynomials, leading to a significant reduction in the number of polynomials required. This work lays the groundwork for future research on the $c$-covering variety and the relationship between $c$-variant spectra of power functions over finite fields. It also opens up new avenues for exploring connections between the $c$-covering variety and the theory of generalized polynomials. Voice conversion aims to alter a source speech signal into a target voice
while maintaining the original content. The primary difficulty in voice
conversion lies in developing a model capable of accurately mapping source
spectrograms into target spectrograms. Recent advancements in diffusion probabilistic
models have demonstrated their effectiveness in voice conversion tasks. In this study,
we introduce DiffSVC, a voice conversion model that employs a diffusion probabilistic
framework. DiffSVC incorporates a deterministic encoder to produce a conditional diffusion
model and a diffusion probabilistic model conditioned on the target spectrogram, allowing
it to learn complex mappings between source and target spectrograms. The model is trained
using a large-scale dataset of paired speech and voice conversion files, and our experiments
demonstrate its ability to produce high-quality voice conversions. When compared to existing
voice conversion methods, DiffSVC achieves superior performance in terms of both subjective
and objective evaluations. The source code for this work is available at https://github.com/whaletoster/DiffSVC. The application of deep learning in medical image analysis has been expanding due to its potential for automatic diagnosis and assistance. However, deep learning models often struggle with domain shift, which occurs when training data exhibits a different distribution than test data. This domain discrepancy significantly hampers model performance, especially in medical imaging, where data scarcity is a significant challenge. To address this limitation, researchers have developed domain transfer techniques that adapt models to target domains by leveraging knowledge from source domains. While previous methods have shown promise, they often struggle with overfitting to target domain features, resulting in suboptimal transferability. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes an unsupervised domain transfer approach that employs a graph convolutional network and utilizes a variational autoencoder to disentangle domain-specific and class-specific features, thereby enhancing transferability and robustness to noise and outliers. Experimental results on three medical image datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this method, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Source code and pre-trained models will be made publicly available to facilitate future research. Further information can be found at https://github.com/ParthM222/DomainTransferUnsupervised. These findings have significant implications for medical imaging, where domain transfer methods can be used to adapt models trained on abundant data to low-resource target domains. This can greatly enhance the reliability and practicality of medical imaging systems. Ultimately, the success of unsupervised domain transfer models relies on their ability to disentangle domain-specific and class-specific features, which is a critical challenge addressed by the proposed approach. By successfully disentangling these features, researchers have achieved significant advancements in medical imaging systems. While this study has focused on medical imaging, the underlying principles can be easily adapted to other applications, including text and vision domains. The field of natural language processing has been revolutionized by word embeddings, which are now a fundamental component of numerous NLP systems. Researchers have been actively developing and enhancing various evaluation metrics for word embeddings to gauge their similarity affinity across languages. These metrics typically rely on specific linguistic features, particularly the similarity between words, analogies, and semantic connections. However, existing evaluation frameworks primarily cater to languages with abundant resources, leaving many under-resourced languages behind. This paper introduces SART, a novel benchmark comprising Tatar language datasets specifically tailored for assessing word embeddings. Given the scarcity of linguistic resources for Tatar, SART was developed using the Tatar Wikipedia corpus, complemented by automatic translations from English. We examine SART alongside three prominent word embedding models, comparing their performance across multiple similarity, analogy, and similarity-based tasks, revealing that SART exhibits a more pronounced performance gap compared to English-based benchmarks. Our analysis sheds light on the performance differences among the models and highlights the importance of SART in evaluating word embeddings for low-resource languages. We establish a key theorem: for a connected graph, G, with maximum node degree, d, and minimum cover number, r, the minimum number of iterations required to solve the chip-burning problem for any given pair of starting and ending nodes is capped at O(r^3 * d^2 + r^2). This problem's solvability iterations directly correlate with integral currents and paths connecting the initial and final nodes. Consequently, the proposed algorithm yields a time-complexity bound of O(r^3 * d^3 + r^2) for graphs with a minimum degree, d > 2, and a time-complexity bound of O(r^3 * (d^2 + log(r))) for graphs with minimum degree, d = 2. These bounds outperform existing methods, with the latter surpassing the current best-known bound of O(r^3 * d^2) established by Cheong, Datta, Datta, and Zickfeld for any given pair of starting and ending nodes. Our findings are further demonstrated through the simulation of chip-burning processes on real-world networks, including the Zegaplex, US Road, and UK Road graphs. This research marks the first time a time-complexity bound for graph chip-burning problems has been achieved for any given pair of starting and ending nodes. Additionally, the proposed algorithm represents the first integral current and cycle chip-burning algorithm capable of handling any given pair of starting and ending nodes. Our simulation results indicate that the proposed algorithm consistently outperforms existing methods, including the state-of-the-art algorithm established by Cheong, Datta, Datta, and Zickfeld. A new framework, referred to as the Deep Adaptive General Polynomial Chaos Expansion (D-GPCE), has been developed to address the complexity associated with solving partial differential equation-based uncertainty problems. This framework integrates machine learning and generalized polynomial chaos methods to adaptively construct a GPCE expansion for a given PDE-based uncertainty problem. Utilizing a mini-data driven semi-supervised learning strategy, D-GPCE first generates an initial surrogate model using labeled training data, then fine-tunes it using a limited set of labeled training data and an extensive amount of unlabeled data. In point cloud processing, data reduction through resampling is a common approach, yet it poses significant risks of compromising data integrity and generating inaccurate results under distorted or noisy conditions. This study presents a novel, hypergraph-based method that effectively mitigates data degradation during resampling, even under distorted or noisy inputs. By representing the data in a hypergraph format, this method leverages the inherent structural information, enabling it to identify critical points that define the shape's topology. Subsequently, an optimized resampling strategy is derived, effectively preserving point cloud data even under distorted or noisy inputs. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that this method yields superior results when compared to existing techniques, providing more accurate, distortion-insensitive, and noise-robust resampled point clouds. Language errors are a persistent problem in AI-driven systems, despite significant advancements in their detection. A key obstacle to overcoming these errors is the widespread assumption that infrequent mistakes are more significant, a notion we test and refute in this study. We examine a corpus of German language evaluation data, comparing the frequencies of both common and uncommon mistakes, and their respective impact on text quality. Our analysis reveals that while infrequent errors are indeed less common, they are crucial for achieving high standards of language quality. Specifically, we found that identifying these errors is essential for producing text of professional or expert-grade quality, a level that remains unaffected by the detection of more frequent errors. Our research offers new insights into the importance of language error detection, and provides valuable information for developing effective evaluation metrics. introducing a modified version of the Heaviest DAG (HDAG) consensus protocol.
Although Tangle 2.0's official whitepaper is extensive, a detailed analysis of HDAG
is lacking. We address this gap by examining its characteristics as a byproduct of this paper.

In HDAG, nodes form a directed acyclic graph by selecting and connecting new edges,
representing distributed consensus among nodes. Each node functions as a proof-of-work
entity, verifying transactions and creating new edges in the process. A node is valid
if it is the end of all its connected edges, known as a leaf. A node becomes a leaf
following a transaction verification process, where the verified transaction is added to the
Tangle.

We identify two types of attacks on HDAG: the first where an attacker modifies the HDAG to become the lightest node, and the second where an attacker forges a new transaction, causing a cascade of changes throughout the Tangle. We demonstrate that HDAG is resistant to both types of attacks, maintaining its properties as a valid consensus mechanism. We also propose a new attack, known as the "cascading fork attack," which exploits weaknesses in the Tangle 2.0 consensus mechanism, making it infeasible to solely rely on HDAG as a robust consensus mechanism. A robust consensus mechanism is defined as one capable of resisting all potential attacks. Consequently, Tangle 2.0's security is compromised by the "cascading fork attack," necessitating the incorporation of additional mechanisms to rectify this vulnerability. We suggest possible solutions to mitigate this issue. 

This paper is structured as follows. First, we introduce Tangle 2.0 and its key components.
We then delve into the specifics of HDAG, examining its properties as a consensus protocol,
before presenting the "cascading fork attack" and demonstrating its implications for Tangle 2.0's security. Finally, we propose potential solutions to mitigate this weakness.

reveals that the most successful writers often work with established directors, and

statistical correlation between a film's budget and its box office performance.

box office success, this study found no evidence to support this claim. Instead, a film's 
box office performance appears to be more closely tied to its release date.

films released during the winter are more successful than those from other times of the 
year, with higher box office returns. Additionally, films with higher production values

This research aims to bridge the gap between simulated and real-world data by providing a reliable and efficient means of evaluating the performance of various 3D reconstruction techniques. This study presents a novel approach to modeling quaternion-valued systems through linear quaternion differential equations (QDEs), exploring their fundamental characteristics and distinctive features. By comparing with linear system models, we establish the uniqueness of the exponential matrix of the fundamental matrix of a QDE and its uniqueness in almost all cases. Furthermore, we extend the concepts of reachable sets and controllability for linear systems to linear quaternion-valued systems. Additionally, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for the controllability of a single quaternion variable in an autonomous QDE. Moreover, we introduce the notion of quaternions differential operator and demonstrate its applications in characterizing controllability, observability, and the existence of singular quaternions in linear quaternion-valued systems. Ultimately, we extend the controllability and observability criteria for quaternion-valued systems to include multiple quaternions. The presented results provide foundational knowledge for future research on nonlinear quaternion-valued systems. The accompanying appendix features a set of essential theorems from quaternion algebra that may be of independent interest. By establishing a direct connection between option values in non-convertible and convertible settings, 
we demonstrate that the pricing formula for convertible options can be calculated using the Heston model's solution. 
Furthermore, we prove that under specific conditions, such an approach remains consistent, even when the market environment becomes more unpredictable. 
Our analysis also extends to situations where the exercise value of the option increases, and we show that under certain assumptions, the pricing formula for convertible options aligns with the Black-Scholes solution, modified for optimal exercise. 
Lastly, we provide numerical examples to illustrate the effects of increased volatility on convertible option prices.

This research is an improvement over Tocquand and Zumbuhl (2021) in that we establish a general framework for pricing convertible options on discrete probability spaces with various levels of volatility, 
whereas their work focused on continuous probability spaces with a single level of volatility.

This study establishes a foundation for co-domain equivalence in complex-valued neural networks. By defining a more practical and efficient framework for measuring the equivalence of network outputs, we demonstrate that existing equivalence measures can be relaxed, resulting in more straightforward and computable checks. Experimental results show that the proposed relaxation can lead to improved generalization performance in certain complex-valued network architectures. Overall, this study provides essential guidelines for the design and evaluation of complex-valued networks. Pretrained multilingual language models, such as Multilingual BERT (mBERT), have been shown to be effective in various language understanding tasks, including machine translation and cross-lingual text classification, across multiple languages. However, the mechanisms behind mBERT's ability to handle these tasks, particularly in low-resource languages, are still not fully understood. In this study, we investigate how mBERT's representations change across languages and how these representations impact its performance in cross-lingual tasks. We propose a new approach, called Align & Forecast, which consists of two stages: aligning mBERT's internal representations with the desired target language and using these aligned representations for cross-lingual forecasting. Our results show that mBERT's alignment and forecasting capabilities are crucial for its success in cross-lingual tasks, and that by leveraging these capabilities, mBERT's performance in low-resource languages can be comparable to that of monolingual BERT. Furthermore, we find that the alignment and forecasting stages are both essential for mBERT's success, and that any significant deviation from these stages leads to a decrease in cross-lingual forecasting performance. Overall, our research provides new insights into the internal workings of mBERT, and offers a practical and efficient way to utilize it for cross-lingual forecasting tasks. In this research, we address the challenge of finding the optimal policy in a constrained Markov decision process (con-MDP). The convergence of algorithms for such problems is often slow, particularly in the exploration phase. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a new method leveraging the concept of natural policy gradients. This involves two key innovations: first, we have designed a policy enhancement rule that efficiently increases the likelihood of convergence by favoring the selection of actions with high expected rewards, and second, a new adaptation of the natural policy gradient theorem enables us to estimate the Fisher information matrix from sampled data. The proposed policy enhancement algorithm is verified to converge at a rapid pace on finite con-MDPs, and we have implemented a practical test to validate its effectiveness in real-world applications such as a resource management system in a data center. The experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms existing methods in terms of both convergence rate and overall performance. Furthermore, our algorithm is shown to produce more efficient policies in a larger number of iterations compared to the state-of-the-art approach. In recent medical imaging research, it has been discovered that density-mapping can be an effective tool in visualizing the three-dimensional distribution of anatomical features extracted from 2D images. This technique is particularly useful in clinical settings, such as assessing the lung function of patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. This study focuses on developing a method for estimating the probability density function from a series of 2D projections, utilizing a trans-dimensional Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler based on sparse Bayesian inference. The proposed approach can be viewed as a hierarchical model that assigns prior probabilities to the coefficients of a linear regression model, resulting in a sparse solution. The study demonstrates the feasibility of this method through simulated data and its potential practical applications in medical imaging. However, it is noted that the trans-dimensional sampler faces significant challenges in identifying the optimal model complexity and may struggle to sample from low-probability regions in the posterior distribution. To address this limitation, a variant of the trans-dimensional sampler has been proposed, incorporating an auxiliary variable to facilitate sampling in these challenging areas. The proposed approach has been found to be a reliable and efficient method for density-mapping and has been successfully applied to a series of simulated and real-world datasets. The associated code is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ambroseh/sparsebayesiandensitymapping. This research has been presented at the 2022 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Medicine, where it has been recognized with the 2022 ambulatory pulmonary disease best paper award. This paper explores a modified version of the 2D chemotaxis--Navier--Stokes system, featuring logistic growth and an exponential chemotaxis response, to examine its large-time behavior under no mass conservation assumption. By employing the Lyapunov functional method, the paper establishes the existence of a global classical solution to the system, and then analyzes the global attractor and pathwise asymptotic behavior under homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions, where the solution converges unifomly and in $L^2(\Omega)$ to a single non-flux boundary solution of a modified logistic equation. Specifically, this solution is unique and exhibits the mass conservation property. Under no-flux boundary conditions, the paper shows the existence of a global attractor in the $H^1(\Omega)$ space, and then analyzes the global attractor's structure and asymptotic behavior, demonstrating the existence of a single non-flux boundary solution of a modified logistic equation as the initial value tends to zero. This solution represents the mass-conservative limit and is unique. Furthermore, the paper investigates the pathwise asymptotic behavior of the solution under both boundary conditions and shows that it converges uniformly and in $L^2(\Omega)$ to this solution. This resolution resolves previously open issues related to the mass conservation and global solvability of the system, and extends the existing results on the system's mass conservation and global solvability under Dirichlet boundary conditions to more general non-flux boundary conditions. Additionally, the paper establishes the global attractor's structure and its finite-dimensionality under both boundary conditions. The study also provides numerical simulations for comparison and validation of the theoretical results. The findings are supported by rigorous mathematical proofs. The advent of smart metering has introduced a new era in monitoring and energy management, where smart meters are used to track energy consumption and disseminate this data to end-users and network operators for optimal energy management. However, the sharing of consumption data by smart meters poses a potential threat to privacy. To mitigate this risk, anomaly detection can be employed to delay the transmission of suspicious energy patterns, ensuring both user privacy protection and data delivery. This study proposes a novel adaptive transmission protocol that enables smart meters to adapt to varying network conditions by dynamically adjusting data transmission rates in response to anomaly identification. To evaluate its performance, simulations were conducted under diverse network conditions. The results indicate that this protocol successfully balances between privacy preservation and data delivery, and it outperforms existing protocols by reducing energy consumption and minimizing packet losses. Furthermore, the simulations demonstrate that the proposed protocol can identify energy anomalies effectively. The protocol also exhibits robustness in various network scenarios and network faults. As a result, the proposed adaptive transmission protocol offers a promising solution for balancing energy management with user privacy in smart metering networks.
