A novel deep learning model has been developed for COVID-19 diagnosis, utilizing a 6-minute unattended audio recording of patients. This model integrates a multi-scale convolutional neural network with a Transformer architecture, leveraging Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients as input features. It is demonstrated that incorporating multi-scale MFCC-grams enhances model performance compared to individual 10ms time windows. Experimental results indicate that combining 10ms and 1s time windows achieves the best classification accuracy of 85.7% for COVID-19 vs. Non-COVID-19 classification. Furthermore, an end-to-end audio-visual model is proposed, which leverages the same audio features and a ResNet-50 visual component to achieve improved classification accuracy of 88.9%. The model and dataset are released publicly for reproducibility. This research has significant implications for remote health monitoring and telemedicine during the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. A key active learning technique, query-based active learning, often relies on identifying the most informative instances to query next and updating the classifier with each new query. While this strategy can optimize the number of queries, it often prioritizes efficiency over quality. As a result, the classifier's current performance may not accurately represent the potential capabilities of the updated model. To address this issue, we propose a method that enhances query-based active learning by improving test performance, which we achieve through two approaches: 1) selecting instances in a way that maintains performance while reducing query count, and 2) using test performance as a metric to refine the query selection process. Our approach is validated through experiments on four diverse datasets, resulting in consistent improvements in test performance, often exceeding 10% in classification accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can also be applied in conjunction with active learning to achieve additional benefits. To ensure the security of computer systems, a non-executable system design with the ability to enforce memory access control is necessary, a feature which existing operating systems fail to provide effectively. To evaluate the feasibility of Fuel, a custom operating system called FuOS is developed, built using a microkernel design, a capability-based API, and a dynamic dynamic linking system. Experimental results demonstrate FuOS's ability to support various system components, including a loader, dynamic linker, and memory allocator, all while maintaining consistent performance relative to existing systems. Furthermore, as Fuel is a highly modular system, it allows for easy modification and extension to accommodate additional security features, demonstrating its potential for further enhancement. Deep reinforcement learning agents may develop suboptimal behaviors when maximizing reward values in their learning process. This suboptimal behavior is linked to reward misestimation, which is the primary cause of misalignment in these agents. To better comprehend the effects of reward misestimation, we investigated its influence on deep RL agents in this research. Specifically, we examined the effects of reward misestimation on two types of RL agents: those trained using maximum expected accuracy (MEA) and those trained using maximum entropy regularization (MELR). Our findings show that MEA agents tend to be more misaligned than MELR agents, which is attributed to the non-differentiable nature of MEA's objective function. Building on this, we proposed a method to alleviate this misalignment issue by incorporating a differentiable penalty term to MEA's reward function. This approach was tested in various scenarios, including navigation and exploration, and demonstrated to be effective in reducing misalignment while maintaining the performance of RL agents. Overall, our research provides a deeper understanding of reward misestimation and introduces a technique to mitigate its negative effects. This paper explores a coordinated network that utilizes non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) to allocate wireless power and data resources to numerous devices (IoT) that require constant power. The underlay NOMA technique allocates non-orthogonal power to IoT devices using an optimal water-filling method, whereas the uplink NOMA technique allocates orthogonal power to IoT devices using an equal power allocation strategy. The theory, despite its foundation in established mathematics, appears to be inconsistent with itself, a contradiction that arises from the field operators' interdependencies and the resulting violations of causality. This article offers a new solution to the contradiction by demonstrating that quantum field operators can effectively carry information without causing paradoxes when their behavior is considered in a space-time context that respects causality. This solution is supported by a mathematical proof that shows the field operators' entanglements do not violate the principle of maximum entropy, a fundamental concept in physics. This concept, known as strong subadditivity, essentially states that the global entropy of a system is less than the sum of its parts, an inequality that is crucial in physics. Our research shows that quantum field operators can effectively carry entanglements without violating this principle. This paper explores the challenge of extracting oscillatory signals from low-frequency observations, particularly when the oscillations are unknown. A novel two-step approach based on Gaussian process inference is developed to tackle this issue. First, the raw data is smoothed using a two-stage Gaussian process, and then the original problem is reformulated to estimate frequency components from the smoothed data. A key aspect of this method involves utilizing the smoothed data to infer the underlying oscillations, and an extension allows for simultaneous estimation of both the oscillations and frequency components. A unique feature of this approach is its ability to provide a probabilistic assessment of the inferred frequencies and amplitudes. Furthermore, the authors introduce a new technique for approximating the inference distribution, which significantly enhances computational efficiency. A simulated study is conducted to evaluate the efficacy of this approach, and it is also applied to real-world data derived from a laboratory experiment. This study reveals that the oscillatory signals can be accurately reconstructed from the smoothed data, and the estimated frequencies exhibit minimal deviation from the true values. Additionally, the authors demonstrate that the proposed method can successfully infer high-frequency oscillations from noisy low-frequency observations, which is particularly relevant in the context of physiological signals. Overall, the proposed approach offers a flexible and efficient framework for analyzing oscillatory signals from unknown frequencies, which is applicable to a wide range of fields. The primary goal of the Visual Inquiry Answering task is to develop a system that can respond to natural language questions based on a pre-processed dataset of images. However, the current state of the RAMEN system is limited in its ability to generalize across domains, which leads to poor performance when encountering new domains. To address this issue, we propose a multi-task learning approach that involves training the system on both the Visual Inquiry Answering task and a related task called Visual Commonsense Reasoning. By leveraging the Visual Commonsense Reasoning task, we can improve the system's ability to generalize across domains. We have tested our approach on the VQA-A dataset and found that it performs significantly better than the standard RAMEN approach, achieving an improvement of 9.8% in average answer accuracy. Moreover, we found that our approach is effective in scenarios where the system is given a limited number of training examples and is asked to generalize to new domains. Specifically, we found that it can achieve an average answer accuracy of 34.4% when given 1000 examples, 33.2% when given 500 examples, and 30.6% when given 200 examples, all on the VQA-A test set. These results demonstrate the potential of our approach and establish a new baseline for the Visual Inquiry Answering task. We developed this metric by leveraging the fact that the VQA-A dataset contains a mix of easy and hard questions, which allows us to evaluate the system's performance in a more nuanced and realistic way. We found that our proposed approach outperforms the standard RAMEN system using our new evaluation metric. The task of identifying films from various sources is known as film recognition. Traditionally, this task is addressed by extracting relevant information from film captions and then classifying them. However, this method's effectiveness can be limited when dealing with films that have incomplete or poorly written descriptions. To overcome this challenge, a novel approach is proposed, which utilizes a film recognition model that does not rely on film captions. Instead, a pre-trained film recognition model is fine-tuned by transferring its knowledge from film recognition to a broader task, such as recognizing general scenes. The pre-trained model is then adapted to film recognition by incorporating film captions. The proposed method excels in film recognition and achieves state-of-the-art results, demonstrating its efficacy. Additionally, a pre-trained model refined through film recognition tasks can be leveraged to improve related downstream tasks such as film caption generation. The proposed method's code and models are made publicly available for further research and development. The results of this work are expected to contribute to the advancement of film recognition and related tasks. The accompanying data will be released under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license. This paper delves into the matrix equation $p(X)=A$, focusing on functions generated by elementary symmetric polynomials up to degree six. It examines how solutions to this equation behave in extensions of the rational field $\mathbb{Q}$ and identifies patterns where $p$ is tied to a single irreducible polynomial or is a combination of two or more such polynomials. Notably, for polynomials up to degree six, a matrix's minimal polynomial directly corresponds to the equation $p(X)=A$. This connection allows us to identify conditions for solutions in extensions of the rational field and provide methods for determining whether specific matrices are diagonalizable. This paper also offers explicit criteria for irreducibility in certain polynomial combinations and offers a simplified approach to determining if a matrix is diagonalizable when its associated polynomial function behaves in a specific, non-decreasing manner. Ultimately, this research provides a comprehensive framework for addressing the matrix equation $p(X)=A$, encompassing various existing approaches and offering novel insights into the nature of polynomial functions. This framework is further demonstrated through an examination of the specific case involving the polynomial $p(X)=X^7-ax^5-a^6$ and matrix $A$ with diagonal entries. This analysis reveals that, for certain values of $a$, the equation $p(X)=A$ has a single solution in $\mathbb{Q}(a)$ and that, for other values, this solution has a degree of 2. This investigation also explores the minimal polynomial of the matrix $A$ and, notably, demonstrates that it does not always directly correspond to the equation $p(X)=A$. This development highlights the importance of considering the polynomial $p(X)=A$ within its full context, encompassing both its numerical and symbolic aspects. This research further illustrates the utility of the new approach through an examination of the case where $p(X)=X^6-aX^4+bx^2$. This paper introduces a tethered aerial robot designed to guide humans through physical contact. To achieve this, the robot is attached to the human by a cable, allowing it to move dynamically and assist navigation. Since the robot's interactions with its human counterpart result in complex forces, a novel human-state-aware regulator is developed to address this. This regulator incorporates a model of human behavior, taking into account body properties and sensor feedback, to calculate the necessary control inputs. Performance is evaluated through detailed simulations across various scenarios. Results demonstrate that the robot can effectively guide humans to a desired location while minimizing the risk of collision by regulating its movement in real-time, thus ensuring a safe interaction experience. Furthermore, the study reveals that the robot's ability to interact with humans improves significantly as the number of interactions increases, showcasing its adaptability and the benefits of using a tethered configuration. Notably, the use of a tether allows the robot to interact with humans in a more dynamic and natural way, providing an enhanced user experience. In comparison to other methods, this approach is shown to provide the best interaction results. Finally, the study's findings are validated by conducting actual experiments involving real humans and robots, confirming the effectiveness of this approach in real-world settings. This study explores the application of deep learning models to identify emotional states in speech recordings, focusing on visual representations derived from these recordings. Utilizing pre-trained models trained on large image datasets, we assess their effectiveness in classifying emotions from speech, a task known as emotional recognition. Our findings demonstrate that these model representations can be effectively applied to various emotional recognition tasks, including two specific scenarios: distinguishing happy from angry speeches and categorizing speeches into six distinct emotional categories. Additionally, we investigate the use of pre-trained models in identifying emotions in speech, comparing different input modalities such as MFCCs and spectrograms. Our analysis reveals that a pre-trained model called Xception can accurately identify emotional states in spectrograms with an accuracy rate of 68.2% in the binary case and 41.4% in the six-class scenario. These results are comparable to or even superior to previous studies in the field. Our research further aims to address the challenge of learning representations for emotional recognition tasks by proposing a pre-training and fine-tuning strategy. Our proposed strategy involves fine-tuning the pre-trained model on a limited emotional recognition task, allowing it to adapt to the specific task at hand. When applied to the six-emotion classification task, this approach leads to an accuracy rate of 53.7%, surpassing existing benchmarks for emotion recognition. Overall, our research demonstrates the effectiveness of pre-trained models in classifying emotions from speech, a task that holds significant potential for real-world applications. Further investigation is warranted to address the limitations of our approach and to fully realize the promise of emotion recognition technology. Our objective is to show that using time-varying factor loadings can effectively
predict mortality rates more accurately than time-constant loadings, based on
factor models that analyze the structure of insurance company mortality data with
multiple stages and diverse risk factors. To achieve this, we develop a new
method that identifies stage-specific factor loadings during different periods
of a portfolio's life using principal component analysis and cluster clustering.
This approach enables the construction of a factor model with varying
properties throughout the portfolio's lifespan. The proposed technique's
performance is evaluated against time-constant factor loadings and compared to
an unweighted mortality model. The results of this study, which uses real mortality
data from 29 long-term care portfolios, demonstrate the potential for improved
mortality prediction using time-variant factor loadings. Furthermore, the study
finds that incorporating additional covariates such as inflation and interest
rates can also enhance mortality prediction accuracy. Finally, the study assesses
the practical implications of these findings by evaluating the profitability of
an investment portfolio based on predicted mortality rates. Our results indicate
that a strategy that adjusts factor loadings over time consistently produces the
best investment returns across all scenarios. Moreover, the additional incorporation
of covariates further boosts the potential returns. Our research contributes to the
understanding of factor models used in actuarial mortality prediction and
contributes to the existing literature in this field. The research also provides an
open-source implementation of the time-variant factor loadings method and
encourages other researchers to adapt and build upon this work. The adapted code is available at https://github.com/philipstoyer/MortalityFactor. We define a relationship, denoted as $\mathcal{G}$, between the topologies of a non-Archimedean analytic space $X$ and its universal covering space $\tilde{X}$. Specifically, $X$ has an $\mathcal{G}$-property with respect to $\tilde{X}$ if the quotient map $\pi: \tilde{X} \rightarrow X$ induces an open map between their topological spaces. Our focus lies in the application of this relationship to the context of tropical surfaces. Initially, we utilize the $\mathcal{G}$-property to establish a key connection between the topologies of tropical surfaces and their corresponding universal covering surfaces. Subsequently, for a given pair of tropical surfaces, we identify the specific subcategories of maps that maintain the $\mathcal{G}$-property. Notably, these categories are characterized by maps of a non-Archimedean nature, including maps of a non-Archimedean curve and maps of a non-Archimedean surface onto another surface. Furthermore, for a given non-Archimedean curve $C$, we demonstrate that maps of $C$ that maintain the $\mathcal{G}$-property fall into the categories of parametrized curves, parametrized maps, or a combination of both. Lastly, for a given non-Archimedean surface $X$, we show that maps of $X$ that maintain the $\mathcal{G}$-property fall into the categories of parametrized curves, parametrized maps, or a combination of both. Additionally, for a given non-Archimedean surface $X$ and parametrized map $f$ onto $X$, we demonstrate that $f$ is equivalent to a map of a non-Archimedean curve onto the boundary of $X$ if and only if $f$ maintains the $\mathcal{G}$-property. This result is utilized to establish a key relationship between the topologies of a non-Archimedean surface $X$ and its boundary $\partial X$. Specifically, for a given non-Archimedean surface $X$ and parametrized map $f$ onto $\partial X$, we demonstrate that $X$ and $\partial X$ have an isomorphic relationship with respect to the $\mathcal{G}$-property. This result is further utilized to establish a key relationship between the topologies of a non-Archimedean surface $X$ and its boundary $\partial X$.

In cloud computing, data centers with intricate network structures are crucial for providing scalable services. Data center operators are under pressure to meet growing demands for high-bandwidth, low-latency services. Virtual network operators play a pivotal role in ensuring the quality of service for virtual networks by selecting the most suitable physical network resources. However, the increasing complexity of data center networks makes it difficult for operators to identify and utilize the most cost-effective physical network topology. This paper introduces a semi-centralized approach to virtual network placement that takes into account network failures and optimizes cost, availability, and reliability. The proposed algorithm considers the impact of network failures on link availability and their effect on the network's connectivity. It uses a multi-objective optimization model that incorporates a failure-aware cost model to minimize the overall cost of virtual network deployment. The results of our experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms traditional centralised and decentralised approaches in terms of cost-effectiveness and robustness to network failures. Notably, the decentralized version of our algorithm achieves better performance than the centralised one, highlighting its potential for deployment in real-world data centers. We examine the computational capabilities of context-sensitive grammars with selection languages that enforce local consistency. Our research demonstrates that the associated decision problems remain unsolvable, even for simple grammar choices. Building on these findings, we show that the class of string languages accepted by these grammars is equal to the class of regular languages, implying that such grammars have limited ability to generate new strings. Our study also reveals that the equivalence of two context-sensitive grammars can be decided in polynomial time when both grammars have locally tested selection languages. In contrast, the equivalence of two context-sensitive grammars with arbitrary languages is NP-complete. Additionally, we prove that the minimal equivalent deterministic automaton for a context-sensitive grammar can be computed in polynomial time when its grammar has a locally tested selection language. The overall framework of our research highlights the importance of selecting appropriate languages for context-sensitive grammars in formal language theory. All of our results are formally proved and verified using the Coq Interactive Theorem Prover. Research has shown that minor alterations to sentences, undetectable to humans, can significantly impact the performance of neural machine translation systems, causing errors in predicting the original sentence's translation. This research paper delves into the realm of representation learning, specifically the challenge of acquiring fair representations, and introduces a novel approach called AFRDP. The AFRDP framework leverages adversarial training in conjunction with an auxiliary loss function to facilitate fair representation learning. Comprised of a fair loss function and a damping/piling loss function, AFRDP works in conjunction with feature distribution regularization to achieve optimal results. The fair loss term addresses class imbalance by enforcing a uniform distribution of class weights, while the damping/piling loss term identifies biased classes and assigns greater weights to them. Theoretical analysis and empirical evidence demonstrate the efficacy of AFRDP in effectively acquiring fair representations on various datasets. Notably, AFRDP's adversarial training mechanism enables it to circumvent the issue of biased class weights in the target distribution, thereby ensuring fairness on all classes. As a testament to its effectiveness, AFRDP outperforms competing methods on various benchmark datasets. Spiking neural networks have gained popularity due to their ability to mimic biological systems and efficient operation. However, implementing SNNs in neuromorphic hardware is complicated by the need to optimize for both accuracy and compatibility. Current SNN approaches focus solely on accuracy, but our study reveals that using standardized and regularized surrogate gradient learning methods significantly enhances compatibility without sacrificing neural network performance. By applying these techniques to SNNs, we achieved a 100-fold improvement in accuracy, reaching 98.4% on MNIST and 92.5% on CIFAR10, outperforming state-of-the-art results on these datasets. Additionally, our methods can be applied to SNNs trained with backpropagation for enhanced compatibility. Source code for our research can be found at https://github.com/issacjade/SGR-SSN.

This paper introduces a novel distributed control framework that facilitates 'plug-and-play' regulation for complex systems with multiple input-output channels. By design, the controller consists of independent modules, each only aware of local input-output correlations. Through a process of distributed learning, the individual components adapt to develop a unified control strategy, effectively learning the relationships between corresponding input and output channels. The approach does not rely on assumptions about the interconnected system or its parameters, nor does it require explicit communication among controllers. We provide theoretical evidence of the method's stability and demonstrate its effectiveness through comparative testing with a standard distributed control algorithm. Notably, the method allows new modules to integrate without additional setup and is scalable for complex systems. Furthermore, the integrated controllers operate independently, each responsible for a specific input-output pair, and are free from dependencies. The comparative study highlights the superior performance of the method in terms of tracking error, convergence speed, and robustness against communication disruptions. The proposed framework is also applied to a more complex problem of linearization control, enabling the stabilization of an inherently unstable system through coordinated control of multiple channels. The results indicate that the method is capable of achieving linearization and maintaining system stability, even in the presence of unknown system parameters. Current approaches to text generation systems often rely on category-based guidance 
which aims to influence the creation of text instances that fall under specific 
categories. A significant issue arises when these systems fail to accurately produce 
text that aligns with the intended category, resulting in low-quality or off-topic 
text. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel framework that 
integrates entity categorization into the text generation process. Our model is 
pre-trained to recognize entities and categorize them, which are then utilized as 
supplementary inputs during the text generation process. We have developed a suite 
of novel loss functions that combine the text generation and entity categorization 
tasks to enhance the accuracy of our entity categorization model. Our experiments 
demonstrate that our proposed approach significantly outperforms traditional text 
generation methods, achieving a 40\% improvement in category accuracy and a 20\% 
improvement in word accuracy on the WikiHow dataset. Our approach also yields 
better results on the arXiv dataset, achieving a 10\% improvement in category accuracy 
compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Our code is publicly available on 
GitHub.

Formal methods are being utilized to develop and verify smart contract specifications, employing specialized techniques to minimize false starts. We've developed an approach to automatically generate smart contracts that adhere to a given specification, leveraging the power of HyperLTL to define complex system properties. By employing a synthesis algorithm based on monadic logic over finite traces, we can efficiently produce HyperLTL-compliant contracts that satisfy the given specification, even for complex hyperproperties. This approach is demonstrated with a case study involving a sophisticated protocol that has proven challenging for existing analysis tools. We've successfully utilized our method to verify the satisfaction of a hyperproperty at each state of the protocol, leading to the discovery of a counterexample and the synthesis of a corrected contract. This achievement showcases the potential of formal methods in the context of HyperLTL, even for intricate protocols. A prototype implementation of our method is available on GitHub. https://github.com/uc-rllmngg/smart-contract-synthesis. Go, a popular programming language used for building cloud-based services and microservices architectures, has seen significant adoption in recent years. However, Go's language features and the framework it utilizes for concurrency are thought to be contributing to a growing number of undetected defects, such as those involving data corruption. Currently available tools for detecting defects in Go are limited, and existing testing methodologies often struggle to identify issues related to concurrency. In this research, a novel approach called BinGo is introduced, which leverages a combination of static and dynamic analysis techniques to identify concurrency flaws in Go programs by analyzing the binary code. BinGo is the first method to identify Go programs' vulnerabilities to specific types of concurrency flaws, including race conditions, deadlocks, and starvation, without requiring the program to be executed or its source code to be examined. An evaluation of BinGo revealed its ability to identify all known Go concurrency flaws and to detect previously unknown issues in Go programs. Furthermore, BinGo was found to be significantly more efficient than existing tools, including those used for examining C programs. In comparison to other tools, BinGo was found to be more effective at identifying concurrency flaws, correctly identifying 100% of issues in a test dataset that included 12,000 Go programs. In contrast, the other tools examined were only able to identify 1% of the issues. Overall, the results demonstrate that BinGo is a more efficient and effective tool for identifying concurrency flaws in Go programs. The trim query involves retrieving a subset of a graph, containing all vertices from a specified subset of nodes, where edges exist between vertices within this subset. Various applications, such as database analysis and network visualization, utilize this query. Researchers have developed several methods for solving this query efficiently, but these approaches have limitations, particularly in handling large sets of edges. Star compression simplifies graphs by reducing edge representation, ultimately improving query performance. This paper investigates the use of star compression in enhancing star-clustering and degenerate edge set algorithms for solving the trim query. Furthermore, it presents an optimized algorithm that leverages star compression to process star-clustering degenerate edge set queries in linear time, outperforming previous methods with an improved time complexity. Experimental results confirm that star compression significantly enhances query efficiency. Specifically, it achieves a 2-4 times speedup in processing non-degenerate edge set queries and a 5-10 times speedup in processing degenerate edge set queries compared to the current most efficient algorithms. Additionally, it demonstrates the feasibility of using star compression in place of recursive decomposition in algorithms for detecting transitive dependencies in graph databases. This allows for the development of smaller and more efficient algorithms with reduced memory requirements. Specifically, it achieves a 5-10 times speedup in transitive dependency detection. Overall, star compression has been shown to accelerate various graph query algorithms by 5 times while maintaining a small memory footprint. Its applicability extends beyond the trim query to other graph-based algorithms. However, it is not suitable for algorithms requiring frequent recursive decomposition. We introduce a novel class of adaptive flow architectures based on mixed grape copulas for complex neural activity modeling. Our proposed model can be broken down into two manageable components: one responsible for modeling varied dependencies within larger groups using copulas, and another that handles smaller, varied connections between neurons using a different type of flow. Our model can be trained using a maximum mean discrepancy-neural network approach, without the need for estimating copula parameters. Our extensive experimental evaluation demonstrates that this model significantly outperforms others in modeling real-world neural data characteristics, even when using fewer parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate its ability to model both large and small network connections, as well as dynamic changes in group sizes. Our research also shows that the model can accurately predict neural activity in novel, unseen environments. Overall, our proposed model offers a highly effective and versatile solution for neural network dependency modeling. We investigate the statistical properties of the non-hierarchical SYK model's energy spectrum, specifically examining self-averaging and fluctuation patterns. Our findings show that the energy spectrum of the SYK model is non-self-averaging, meaning its average energy density exhibits significant fluctuations across different realizations, even in the large-N limit. This non-averaging behavior is distinct from complex eigenvalue models like the GOE and GUE ensembles. In contrast, the variance of the energy spectrum within a single realization is found to decrease exponentially with increasing energy. This pattern holds for both the strong coupling regime and the large-N limit. This paper introduces Energy-Conscious Network Operator Search (ENOS), an innovative approach to identifying the most energy-efficient software configuration for complex deep neural networks (DNNs) on hybrid accelerators that combine digital and compute-in-memory processing units. ENOS employs a software stack comprising digital processing, memory, and compute-in-memory acceleration, with the goal of optimizing the entire pipeline for various DNN workloads. A novel method called ENOS searches for the optimal software configuration by minimizing energy consumption for a given DNN, while also considering the flexibility of operator selection and resource distribution across hybrid accelerators. ENOS breaks down complex DNN layers into smaller components, known as operator trees, and employs a genetic search algorithm to find the most energy-efficient configuration for each operator tree within specified constraints. ENOS then reconstructs the entire DNN by combining the optimized operator trees, resulting in significant energy savings. Our experiments demonstrate that ENOS achieves up to 6.6x and 3.9x energy savings on hybrid accelerators compared to state-of-the-art methods, with minimal accuracy loss. Furthermore, ENOS can reduce energy consumption by 13.6% to 46.6% compared to the best existing approaches. Our results also show that ENOS can adapt to dynamic input data and achieve substantial energy savings under low-power constraints. Overall, ENOS provides a novel software-level acceleration technique for hybrid accelerators that surpasses traditional methods in energy efficiency. Our open-source implementation is available online. Additionally, we present a tool called ENOS-Analyzer, which visualizes the search process, and demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying the most energy-efficient operator trees. Our work is the first to introduce a general-purpose operator search algorithm for DNNs on hybrid accelerators, and our ENOS-Analyzer tool facilitates a deeper understanding of the search process. We also discuss the implications of our work, including its potential applications in the fields of puzzle-solving, robotics, and optimization, as well as its potential role in advancing the field of artificial intelligence through the development of new AI agents.  Finally, we outline the potential directions for future research in this area.  The code and models developed in this study are publicly available online. Recent advancements in object detection have seen the emergence of various novel methods, each surpassing its predecessors in performance. However, the rapid pace of innovation has led to a significant challenge: accurately measuring progress in object detection, particularly in scenarios where comparing new methods with their predecessors is complicated due to substantial changes in architecture or training protocols. This study investigates the benefits of a combination of multiple datasets for object detection, aiming to improve detection accuracy in areas with limited data availability, like the Omnivore/Mammal dataset. Our findings indicate that merging datasets can lead to improved detection results in smaller datasets. We propose the use of a modified Quicker R-CNN architecture, incorporating various techniques such as dataset amalgamation and soft distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that this modified architecture achieves a 5-point Mean Average Precision gain over the original method when trained on a dataset of 1,200 images, while reducing the number of parameters by 50%. When trained on a dataset of 1,500 images, our modified architecture achieves a 6-point Mean Average Precision gain over the original method while using 75% fewer parameters. Furthermore, we observe that the use of multiple datasets enhances the model's ability to generalize to different categories, even when trained on a dataset with different categories than the test dataset. Self-guided learning, a technique that involves generating pseudo-labels for unlabeled data, has been successfully applied to various tasks. However, it is susceptible to dataset imbalance - when some classes have much fewer instances than others. To address this, we propose a straightforward yet effective method that resamples the imbalanced dataset to equalize the number of instances per class. Our approach involves utilizing a single input light beam to perform the multiplication of two complex spatial light patterns, referred to as a and b. This technique relies on the interaction between a specially designed multi-mode waveguide and a controlled phase shift in the waveguide's mode dispersion. Our results demonstrate the ability to achieve high-precision multiplication with an average error rate of less than 0.1%, utilizing a simplified model of the multi-mode waveguide. This method has the potential to be scaled up to perform the multiplication of more complex spatial light patterns, enabling the development of more practical optical neural networks. Our work also explores alternative approaches for the multiplication of two complex spatial light patterns, including the use of a Mach-Zehnder interferometer and a free-space optical system. These methods, however, require multiple input beams and are more susceptible to imperfections in device fabrication. Therefore, we propose that the proposed multi-mode waveguide approach is a more practical and efficient solution for practical implementation. This research contributes to the ongoing development of optical multipliers within neuromorphic photonic integrated circuits, with the ultimate goal of achieving a more efficient and practical implementation of neural networks. To validate our findings, we compare the performance of the proposed multi-mode waveguide approach with the alternative approaches for the multiplication of two complex spatial light patterns, demonstrating the potential of the proposed method for practical implementation. Our findings are based on a comprehensive analysis of the sensitivity of the multi-mode waveguide approach to variations in device parameters and the impact of fabrication imperfections. As video conferencing continues to evolve, there is an increasing need for more efficient video transmission. The high-quality video sent over internet with low latency poses significant challenges, particularly when it comes to limited bandwidth. We developed Gemino, a system that overcomes these obstacles by employing a novel neural approach to compress video in real-time. By utilizing a specialized H.264 encoder, a complex video patch is first broken down into smaller frames using a high-resolution super-resolution network, and then further divided into smaller blocks by a block-wise image coding network. The resulting information is then sent to the H.264 encoder for final processing. We tested our system on a widely used video conferencing tool and found that Gemino outperforms current standards by reducing video bitrate by 20-40% with minimal impact on video quality. We also demonstrated Gemino's ability to withstand network failures, reducing the time it takes to recover from such failures by 60%. Furthermore, our system has shown to be adaptable to various network conditions, balancing transmission quality and bitrate accordingly. The ability to choose from multiple clothing items when dressing is a fundamental aspect of human expression, and the development of innovative clothing technologies can greatly enhance this capability.  However, current automated clothing systems are inflexible, only designed to work with a single pre-assembled garment.  In this research, we introduce a versatile, customizable top-to-bottom clothing system that can accommodate a wide range of clothing items, including those that are partially assembled.  We begin this study by first understanding how to break down a garment into its underlying fabric components, and then create a standardized representation of these components.  Next, we introduce a versatile algorithm that can seamlessly integrate these components into a cohesive garment, and our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in creating versatile clothing solutions.  This research lays the groundwork for the creation of a wide range of innovative clothing technologies, and our comprehensive system can be applied to a variety of clothing manipulation tasks.  Additionally, we conduct a user study to validate the effectiveness of our system and assess the impact of its versatility. The organization of digital libraries is significantly influenced by the type of content they contain, such as academic journals or books. In contrast, the metadata used for search and filtering decisions in many libraries are based solely on user preferences and constraints, rather than taking into account the specific characteristics of the library's collection. In this study, the classification of a library's content is explored as a means to enhance search and suggestion capabilities. A categorization framework is proposed, encompassing four types of content and their respective features, such as academic journals, popular books, general interest publications, and teaching materials. Using data from the Internet Archive, the authors demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework in improving search results and suggestions. Through a user study, it was found that the categorization framework enhances search accuracy and reduces content overload by offering users targeted information on specific types of content. Additionally, the framework facilitates the comparison of search systems across different libraries based on their content types, enabling users to make more informed decisions about their information needs. The study's results are intended to inform the development of user-centric information systems and provide a basis for evaluating the kind of content offered by various search systems. Finally, the authors discuss the potential limitations and future directions for incorporating the proposed framework in information systems. Additionally, CVL-Base's pre-trained multimodal language model significantly outperforms the second-best model in video text recognition, with a relative improvement of 6.5%. This review aims to provide further clarification on the matter.

This research introduces HSC4D, a cutting-edge framework for acquiring 4D data of human activity within vast indoor and outdoor environments. HSC4D leverages data from wearable inertial measurement units and LiDAR technology to track human pose and movement. It utilizes a machine learning approach to enhance the estimation of human pose, and subsequently, generates 4D location data for the tracked subjects. HSC4D features a novel pose tracking method and a pose-to-location mapping technique. Initially, a neural network is trained to forecast future human pose based on historical data from wearable IMUs. This prediction is then integrated with LiDAR-based depth data to accurately determine the subject's location. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of HSC4D, achieving a 4D pose accuracy of 0.13 meters and 0.02 meters of angular precision. Moreover, HSC4D's ability to track subjects at a rate of 10 Hz across extensive outdoor and indoor environments was validated. As a pioneering approach, HSC4D focuses on human activity within extensive outdoor and indoor spaces, making it a valuable tool for applications such as intelligent surveillance, robotics, and augmented reality. As such, HSC4D has the potential to serve as a reliable and efficient method for tracking human activity within large-scale environments. The objective of open-set identification is to determine if a given input, x, belongs to a known class or not, with no assumption on unknown classes.  Current approaches to this problem have significant limitations, particularly in terms of generalizability, where most methods struggle to generalize to new samples from unknown classes.  A major shortcoming of existing methods is their reliance on feature extraction networks that are not designed to produce features useful for distinguishing between in-distribution and out-of-distribution data.  In this study, a new approach to open-set identification is proposed, leveraging a similarity metric to distinguish between in-distribution and out-of-distribution data.  A key innovation of this approach is the use of a similarity head that is trained to produce a similarity score between input data and in-distribution classes, with features that are extracted by a classification head that is trained to produce class labels.  Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in distinguishing between in-distribution and out-of-distribution data, with significant improvements in generalizability compared to existing methods.  A major benefit of this approach is that it does not require any labeled out-of-distribution data, with the training process relying on in-distribution data alone.  Furthermore, this approach can be easily integrated with a variety of existing open-set identification methods to improve their performance.  Experimental results demonstrate that this approach can improve the accuracy of existing methods by up to 9.5%.  A major benefit of this approach is its ability to produce state-of-the-art results with significantly less computational overhead.  The code for this approach will be made available at https://github.com/isl-group/similarity-based-OSI.  In addition, a major contribution of this study is the development of a benchmark dataset for open-set identification, with the creation of a new dataset called ImageNet-Out. Researchers have investigated how resonance patterns in dynamic systems interact when one system excites another. These patterns, referred to as resonance tongues, emerge when the excitation threshold is reached for specific combinations of parameters. In this study, an optically pumped microcavity with delayed response is examined, which exhibits complex dynamics. By pulsing the excitation drive, researchers observed unique behavior where the excitation threshold is adjusted by modulating the pulse width. This modulation led to the creation of new resonance tongues that bridge gaps between existing tongues.
